title: Does the Message End on a One-Bit Code
statement:
A tiny protocol has three codes. The short code is a single bit 0. The two long codes are two bits each: 10 and 11.

You get a bit array bits that is a valid message made of these codes, and its last bit is always 0. Read the message from the start. Return true if the final code is the one-bit 0, and false if that last 0 is the second half of a 10.

examples.why: It reads as 11 then 0. The last code is the one-bit 0.
It reads as 0 then 10. The last 0 belongs to the two-bit code.
11 then 10. Just checking that the bit before the end is 1 would be right here, but not in the first example, where that 1 was the second half of 11.

constraints: bits ends with 0 and is a valid message
hints: A 1 always starts a two-bit code, and a 0 at a code boundary is always the one-bit code. So the message can be read in only one way.
Walk an index from the start: on a 1 jump two places, on a 0 jump one. Where do you land just before the end?
Faster to think about: only the 1s directly before the final 0 matter. If their count is even they pair up among themselves; if it is odd, one of them grabs the last 0.

explain.intuition:
The decoder never has a choice: a 1 must start a two-bit code, and a 0 seen at a code boundary must be a one-bit code. So simulate it. Keep an index i and jump by bits[i] + 1. If you land exactly on the last position, the last code is the one-bit 0; if you jump over it, the last 0 was eaten by a 10.

There is a shortcut. Any 0 before the end resets the reading, because a code boundary always follows it. So only the unbroken block of 1s right before the final 0 matters. An even number of them pair into 11 codes; an odd number leaves one 1 to pair with the final 0.
pitfalls: Only looking at bits[n − 2]. In [1, 1, 0] it is 1, yet the answer is true.
Counting all 1s in the array instead of only the block directly before the final 0.

solutions.title: Decode from the start
solutions.idea: A 1 starts a two-bit code, a 0 is a one-bit code. Jump through the codes and check where you land.

solutions.title: Parity of the trailing ones
solutions.idea: Count the 1s directly before the final 0. An even count pairs off into 11 codes; an odd count leaves a 10 at the end.
solutions.time: O(n) worst case, often much less

followups: Return the full list of decoded codes instead of only the last one.
Now the message may be invalid. How do you detect that?
